questions.question: What does External Services let you do that a plain Flow HTTP Callout action doesn't by itself?
options: Make callouts without a Named Credential
Register an external API's OpenAPI spec once and get reusable invocable actions usable from both Flow and Apex
Skip authentication entirely
Avoid the need for any API specification
questions.explanation: External Services turns a registered OpenAPI spec into reusable invocable actions — the declarative equivalent of hand-writing a callout wrapper class.

questions.question: A support admin needs to maintain a simple external callout long after the project ends, with no Apex experience. Which approach fits best?
options: A custom Apex REST class with no documentation
A Queueable Apex job
A Flow HTTP Callout action or External Services action, since it's admin-editable without code
A Batch Apex class scheduled nightly
questions.explanation: Declarative tools are specifically valuable when non-developers need to own and maintain the integration.

questions.question: What do declarative HTTP Callout actions in Flow still require for authentication?
options: Nothing, Flow callouts bypass authentication
A hardcoded API key pasted into a Flow variable
A separate login screen shown to the Flow user
A Named Credential, same as an Apex callout
questions.explanation: Declarative tools don't bypass the platform's authentication model — they still rely on a Named Credential to call out securely.

questions.question: What's a sign that a declarative (Flow/External Services) integration has outgrown its approach and should move to Apex?
options: It successfully completed its first callout
It now needs complex branching, retries, or non-trivial payload transformation that's hard to maintain declaratively
It's being used by more than one Flow
The external API added a new field
questions.explanation: Declarative tools are great for straightforward request/response logic; growing complexity is a signal to reconsider Apex.

questions.question: What happens if a Flow's HTTP Callout action fails and there's no Fault Path configured?
options: Flow automatically retries forever
Flow silently converts it to a success
The failure isn't explicitly handled — the same gap as an Apex callout with no catch block
Salesforce disables the Flow permanently
questions.explanation: Just like Apex needs a catch block, Flow needs an explicit Fault Path — skipping it leaves the error path unhandled.
